text: There are n children in a line. Each one has a rating. Every child gets at least one candy. If a child has a higher rating than a neighbor, they must get more candies than that neighbor. Return the minimum total number of candies.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the rule only talks about direct neighbors, and it only works one way: higher rating means more candy. So if two neighbors have the same rating, there's no rule between them at all. One can have more, one can have less. Is that right?

Good. Then I want to flag one thing early. Each child has two rules, one for the left neighbor and one for the right. The two-sided rule is what makes this hard, but each one-sided rule is easy. So my guess is I can solve each side alone, then combine them. Are there any constraints on the input size?
n goes from one to two times ten to the fourth. Ratings go from zero to two times ten to the fourth.

So I want something close to linear time. Quick check on the examples. One, zero, two: the middle child is lowest and gets one, both ends are higher so they each need two — total five. Matches. One, two, two: the third child ties the second, so there's no rule and it just gets one — total four. Matches too.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach starts everyone at one and keeps scanning, bumping any child who breaks a rule, until nothing changes. It's correct, but on a long falling slope each pass fixes only one step, so it's quadratic. This problem reminds me of a two-sweep greedy pattern: build a lower bound from each side with one scan, then combine them, because the answer at each spot depends on both the left and the right. So: one greedy pass left to right for the left rule, one pass right to left for the right rule, and take the max.

Here's the plan. One: everyone starts at one candy. Two: left to right, a child who beats its left neighbor gets one more than that neighbor. Three: right to left, a child who beats its right neighbor gets the max of what it has and one more than that neighbor. Then sum. Why the minimum? Each pass measures a rising run that any valid answer must cover, so each is a lower bound, and their max is a lower bound we can reach. One thing worth flagging — the second pass must go right to left, so the right neighbor is already final; otherwise two, one, zero gives five instead of six. A constant-space version exists, but it's trickier. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. A candy array of ones, a forward loop for the left rule, a backward loop for the right rule, then accumulate. One thing worth flagging — the max in the second loop is about correctness. Pass one may already have given a child a big number from a long climb on the left, and plain assignment throws that away: on zero, one, two, zero, the two drops from three to two, and the total is six instead of seven. Two small details: the backward loop starts at n minus two, since it reads the right neighbor. And both checks are strictly greater — with greater-or-equal, zero, zero returns three instead of two.

Let's dry-run with a peak, so the two passes disagree: one, three, five, four, three, two, one — expected eighteen. Pass one gives the left climb one, two, three. The row that matters in pass two is the peak: the left side says three, but the slope down from it is five long, so the max makes it five. The sum is eighteen. Matches. Corner cases: equal ratings in the middle reset to one. A single child gets one. One then zero needs three, where pass one alone says two. A strictly rising line of five gives fifteen.
How sure are you that this is the true minimum?

The lower-bound argument is the real proof. But I also checked it against a brute force that tries every assignment for n up to seven — one hundred twenty-one thousand, eight hundred forty-four cases, zero mismatches. And against the repeat-until-stable version on twenty thousand random cases up to two hundred children. Zero mismatches there too.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear: two passes plus one sum. Space is linear for the candy array. On fifty thousand random children it runs in about half a millisecond. The worst-case total is a strictly rising line, n times n plus one over two — about one point two five billion at fifty thousand children, still below the int limit, so summing with an int is safe. Oh, one more thing — if you want constant extra space, there's a one-pass version that counts up-slopes and down-slopes as triangle sums. The tricky part is the peak, which belongs to both slopes. For an interview, the two-pass version is much easier to explain and to prove.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You split the two-sided rule into two one-sided rules, and explained why the second pass has to go right to left. You proved it's the minimum, not just valid: each pass is a lower bound, and their max is both a lower bound and reachable. And you showed the max in pass two is about correctness, plus why equal ratings reset to one. Good work.
